index.title: {n} instruments, one line each
index.lead: Choose a family, or search. Every line is a real deal, dated and sourced; {n_used} are already in use, and Standard Tokens is designed by Perfect Nations. Open a line for how it works and its source.

families.name: Sovereign bonds
families.line: Borrowing on the capital markets in the nation’s own name.

items.name: International Sovereign Bond
items.headline: Borrow dollars or euros from investors worldwide.
items.how: The treasury sells bonds abroad in a hard currency and pays a fixed coupon until it repays in full.
items.label: investor demand of nearly $6B

items.name: Debut Eurobond
items.headline: A nation’s first bond on the international market.
items.how: A first issue sets the nation’s price with global investors and opens the market for every later bond.
items.label: orders above $5B across two tranches

items.name: Local-Currency Infrastructure Bond
items.headline: Borrow at home, in the currency the budget earns.
items.how: Sold through the central bank to local banks, pension funds and savers, often tax-free to draw demand.
items.label: accepted, after KSh 288.7B of bids

items.name: Retail Treasury Bond
items.headline: Citizens lend to their own government, in small amounts.
items.how: Sold through banks and apps in small denominations, it turns household savings into public investment.
items.label: awarded at 6.875% a year

items.name: Retail Mobile Bond
items.headline: Any citizen can buy a government bond by phone.
items.how: A government bond sold in small amounts through mobile money, so ordinary savers can own a share of public finance.
items.label: the minimum to invest, by phone

items.name: Diaspora Bond
items.headline: A bond sold to citizens living abroad.
items.how: The nation borrows from its own people overseas, who often accept a lower return to invest at home.
items.label: Nigeria’s first diaspora bond

items.name: Panda Bond
items.headline: Borrow in yuan, in China’s onshore market.
items.how: A foreign government sells yuan bonds inside China and reaches a new pool of investors.
items.label: the Republic’s first panda bonds
items.source: Ministry of Finance of Indonesia, July 2026

items.name: Samurai Bond
items.headline: Borrow in yen from Japanese investors.
items.how: Bonds in yen, sold in Tokyo, add Japanese investors to the nation’s lenders.
items.label: sovereign borrowing in Japan

items.name: Sovereign Sukuk
items.headline: Islamic finance: returns from real assets, not interest.
items.how: Investors receive returns from state assets held in trust, under Islamic law, in place of interest.
items.label: three tranches, orders of $4.5B
items.source: Ministry of Finance of Indonesia, June 2024

families.name: Labelled bonds
families.line: Bonds whose money is ring-fenced for a purpose.

items.name: Social Bond
items.headline: Bond money ring-fenced for homes, schools and clinics.
items.how: The proceeds can be spent only on eligible social projects, reported to investors each year.
items.label: for affordable homes

items.name: Sustainability-Linked Bond
items.headline: Miss the national climate target and the coupon rises.
items.how: The money is general budget money, but the interest rate steps up if the nation misses targets it set in advance.
items.label: the first of its kind

items.name: Sovereign Green Bond
items.headline: Bond money ring-fenced for clean energy and climate.
items.how: The proceeds finance eligible green projects under a published framework, with allocation reports to investors.
items.label: in the first issuance

items.name: Sovereign Blue Bond
items.headline: Bond money ring-fenced for oceans and fisheries.
items.how: A green bond for the sea: the proceeds fund marine protection and sustainable fisheries, here with a World Bank guarantee behind it.
items.label: the world’s first

items.name: Sovereign Green Sukuk
items.headline: Green bond finance that complies with Islamic law.
items.how: A sukuk is backed by assets rather than interest; the green sukuk spends every dollar on eligible climate projects.
items.label: the world’s first

items.name: Sustainable Bond
items.headline: One bond for social and environmental spending together.
items.how: The proceeds are tied to both social and environmental spending under the nation’s sustainable bond framework.
items.label: orders three times the size

items.name: City Green Bond
items.headline: A city borrows abroad for its own green projects.
items.how: A city issues under its own credit, with development banks as anchor investors to draw others in.
items.label: the city’s first international green bond

items.name: Climate Transition Bond
items.headline: Bond money for heavy industry’s path to low carbon.
items.how: The proceeds finance the shift of steel, chemicals and power toward net zero, under a government framework.
items.label: accepted at the first auction, 10 years at 0.7%
items.source: Ministry of Finance of Japan, February 2024

families.name: Capital markets
families.line: Shares, securitisations and hedges that bring private savings in.

items.name: IPO Cornerstone Investment
items.headline: A development bank anchors a listing, so others buy in.
items.how: A cornerstone investor commits before the public offer, giving other investors confidence in the price.
items.label: Maynilad, water for about 10.5 million people

items.name: State Asset Listing
items.headline: The state sells shares in a company on the stock market.
items.how: Listing part of a state company raises money, widens ownership and brings market discipline.
items.label: IFC and EBRD in the Banque du Caire offering

items.name: Asset-Backed Securities
items.headline: Small loans bundled into securities investors can buy.
items.how: A lender pools many small loans and sells securities backed by their repayments, freeing it to lend again.
items.label: micro-loans for women entrepreneurs

items.name: Joint Bond Issuance
items.headline: Small lenders issue one bond together to reach the market.
items.how: Several lenders pool their issue so investors can buy at a size none could reach alone.
items.label: the first public-market joint issuance

items.name: Mortgage Refinance Bond
items.headline: Long-term money so banks can offer affordable home loans.
items.how: A national refinance company borrows on the bond market and lends long to banks for mortgages.
items.label: first tranche, oversubscribed more than fourfold

items.name: Currency Hedging Facility
items.headline: Protection from exchange-rate swings, so foreign investors commit.
items.how: A development bank and the central bank offer long-dated currency hedges that markets will not provide.
items.label: of currency hedging, announced at COP30

items.name: Standard Tokens
items.headline: A citizen-scale share in one basic living standard.
items.how: Designed by Perfect Nations: small units of finance, priced by region, each tied to one of the seven basic living standards. Pending compliance review.
items.label: pending compliance

families.name: Equity and funds
families.line: Ownership capital: shares, stakes and the funds that hold them.

items.name: Sovereign Wealth Fund
items.headline: The nation saves and invests its resource wealth.
items.how: Oil and mineral revenue goes into ring-fenced funds for stability, future generations and infrastructure.
items.label: total assets, across three ring-fenced funds

items.name: Sovereign Stake in a Project
items.headline: The nation owns part of its flagship project.
items.how: A blended fund pays for the government’s equity, so the nation shares in the profits without new debt.
items.label: for the Government’s 24% of a green hydrogen project

items.name: Growth Equity
items.headline: A minority stake that funds a company’s expansion.
items.how: Investors buy shares in a fast-growing firm and share in its upside.
items.label: for green hydrogen and ammonia plants

items.name: Subordinated Loan
items.headline: Capital that ranks last, so a bank can lend more.
items.how: Repaid after other creditors, it counts toward the bank’s capital and lifts what it can lend.
items.label: for women-led microenterprises

items.name: Green Bank
items.headline: A national bank that keeps green credit flowing locally.
items.how: Public and climate-fund equity capitalise a bank that lends to households and firms for energy, water and resilience.
items.label: Green Climate Fund equity

families.name: Project finance
families.line: Projects repaid from their own revenues.

items.name: Project Finance
items.headline: Lenders are repaid from the project’s own earnings.
items.how: A company set up for one project borrows against its future sales, such as power sold under a long contract.
items.label: senior debt for a 1.1 GW wind farm

items.name: Public-Private Partnership
items.headline: A private partner builds and runs a public asset.
items.how: The partner finances, builds and operates under a long concession; the asset then passes to the state.
items.label: IFC loan and hedging for the national water carrier

items.name: Mining Project Finance
items.headline: Loans for a mine, with the state’s share guaranteed.
items.how: Senior loans fund construction; a guarantee covers the province’s equity so it keeps its stake.
items.label: Reko Diq copper and gold, first phase

items.name: City Loan
items.headline: Development banks lend straight to a city.
items.how: A municipality borrows on its own balance sheet, tied to reforms that raise its revenue.
items.label: for Fortaleza’s fiscal reform and urban growth

items.name: Blended Infrastructure Loan
items.headline: Commercial and concessional money together, for hard places.
items.how: A concessional slice lowers the cost and risk, so commercial money can follow into fragile markets.
items.label: shared telecom towers, with up to $29M concessional

families.name: Impact investment
families.line: Capital that targets a measured social or environmental return.

items.name: Impact Investment Fund
items.headline: Pooled capital for a nation’s green and social priorities.
items.how: Public and private investors commit to one fund that takes stakes in projects and reports their impact.
items.label: EU investment toward a $1B blended fund

items.name: Blended Finance Platform
items.headline: Public capital and currency cover that bring private investors in.
items.how: The state takes the risks private investors will not, such as currency swings, so they invest in the nation’s priorities.
items.label: mobilised in the first year

items.name: First-Loss Guarantee
items.headline: Public money takes the first losses, so lenders step in.
items.how: A concessional window absorbs the first share of any defaults, so a bank lends to borrowers it once refused.
items.label: in ariary; 30% for women-led firms

items.name: Local-Currency Microfinance Loan
items.headline: Small-business credit in the currency borrowers earn.
items.how: Lending in local currency removes exchange-rate risk from the smallest borrowers.
items.label: in birr; half for women-owned firms

items.name: Risk-Sharing Facility
items.headline: A development bank shares the losses on small-business loans.
items.how: The bank keeps lending to small firms because part of any loss falls on the development bank.
items.label: senior loan and risk-sharing for small firms

items.name: Gender-Lens Investment
items.headline: Capital aimed at closing the gap for women.
items.how: Investment tied to lending for women, such as home loans for women buyers.
items.label: housing finance for women

families.name: Pay for results
families.line: Money moves only when results are verified.

items.name: Outcome Bond
items.headline: Investors earn more as verified results arrive.
items.how: The principal is protected; the return rises with the result, here the carbon a replanted forest removes.
items.label: Amazon reforestation

items.name: Conservation Outcome Bond
items.headline: The return rises as an endangered species recovers.
items.how: Investors forgo coupons; a success payment follows the measured growth of the rhino population.
items.label: tied to black rhino numbers

items.name: Carbon-Linked Outcome Bond
items.headline: The coupon is paid from carbon credits a project earns.
items.how: Investors give up fixed interest for a share of the carbon credits that clean cookstoves generate.
items.label: of private capital for clean cookstoves

items.name: Development Impact Bond
items.headline: Investors fund the work; outcome payers repay them for results.
items.how: Investors pay for delivery up front. A donor or foundation repays them, with a return, only once an independent evaluator verifies the results.
items.label: of the learning target

items.name: Social Impact Bond
items.headline: The same deal at home, with the government paying for results.
items.how: Investors fund a programme; the government repays them only for the outcomes it wanted, here formal jobs found and kept.
items.label: paid for jobs found, not for training given

items.name: Program-for-Results
items.headline: A loan disbursed only as agreed results are verified.
items.how: Each tranche is tied to a disbursement-linked indicator, such as pupils reaching a learning level, and is released when that result is verified.
items.label: for primary school learning

items.name: Results-Based Payments
items.headline: A set price for each verified unit of result.
items.how: A buyer pays a fixed price per verified unit: a tonne of emissions avoided, a child vaccinated, a home connected.
items.label: paid for 3.89 million tonnes of emissions reduced

families.name: Guarantees and insurance
families.line: A stronger balance sheet stands behind the deal.

items.name: Partial Credit Guarantee
items.headline: A guarantor covers part of the debt, so banks lend more.
items.how: A development bank guarantees part of the repayments, which lowers the lenders’ risk and the borrower’s cost.
items.label: behind a $1.2B railway loan

items.name: Payment Guarantee
items.headline: A guarantee on a state buyer’s promise to pay.
items.how: Suppliers sell on longer terms because a development bank stands behind the state company’s payments.
items.label: behind LNG import payments

items.name: Policy-Based Guarantee
items.headline: A guarantee that lets a nation borrow commercially, for less.
items.how: A development bank guarantees a commercial loan tied to reforms, cutting the rate and lengthening the term.
items.label: 15 years; 95% of debt service covered

items.name: Infrastructure Guarantee
items.headline: A guarantee that draws private lenders into infrastructure.
items.how: The guarantee lets private lenders finance public infrastructure on longer, cheaper terms than they would alone.
items.label: for infrastructure and private investment

items.name: Political Risk Insurance
items.headline: Cover against expropriation, inconvertibility and unrest.
items.how: An insurer pays investors if a named political risk stops the project, so they invest where they otherwise would not.
items.label: for new water treatment plants
items.source: U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, December 2024

items.name: Breach-of-Contract Cover
items.headline: Investors are paid if a state breaks its contract.
items.how: MIGA pays the investor if the state fails to honour agreed terms, such as payments for power.
items.label: for rural electrification

items.name: Small-Business Credit Guarantee
items.headline: Guarantees on small-business loans, so banks lend to them.
items.how: The facility guarantees up to 80 percent of each loan, capped at $1 million, through local banks.
items.label: up to 80% of each loan

items.name: Local-Currency Guarantee
items.headline: Lets a borrower raise money in the currency it earns.
items.how: A guarantor backs a bond in local currency, so the borrower carries no exchange-rate risk.
items.label: Kenya’s first green bond, repaid in full

families.name: Development loans and the IMF
families.line: Long-term, low-cost lending from development banks and the IMF.

items.name: Investment Project Financing
items.headline: A loan for one defined project, paid out as it is built.
items.how: The development bank pays for works and services as they are delivered, under its safeguards.
items.label: climate resilience and water security

items.name: Budget Support
items.headline: Budget money released as agreed reforms are passed.
items.how: The money goes to the treasury once prior actions, such as a new law or tariff, are complete.
items.label: a $1B grant and a $500M credit

items.name: Concessional Loan
items.headline: Decades to repay, at very low interest.
items.how: Concessional windows lend for decades, with long grace periods, to the nations that need it most.
items.label: home loans for at least 40,000 households

items.name: IMF Programme
items.headline: IMF money, released review by review, to steady the economy.
items.how: Each tranche follows a review of agreed targets for the budget, debt and reserves.
items.label: about $3.7B disbursed by April 2026

items.name: Resilience and Sustainability Facility
items.headline: Long-term IMF money for climate reform.
items.how: Affordable, long-maturity IMF financing that sits beside a core programme and rewards climate reforms.
items.label: beside its core programme

items.name: Flexible Credit Line
items.headline: A precautionary IMF line, there if a shock comes.
items.how: Strong economies pre-qualify for a large line they can draw at once, and most never draw it.
items.label: two years, precautionary

families.name: Debt conversions
families.line: Costly debt refinanced; the savings go to people and nature.

items.name: Debt-for-Nature Swap
items.headline: Cheaper debt in exchange for protecting nature.
items.how: Guarantees and insurance let the nation exchange costly bonds for a cheaper loan; the savings fund conservation for years.
items.label: of bonds exchanged to protect the Galápagos
items.source: Ministry of Economy and Finance of Ecuador, May 2023

items.name: Debt-for-Climate-Resilience Swap
items.headline: Savings from cheaper debt build climate defences.
items.how: Multilateral guarantees replace costly debt with cheaper debt, and the savings are spent on resilience: here water and sewerage.
items.label: the world’s first for resilience

items.name: Debt-for-Education Swap
items.headline: Savings from cheaper debt build schools.
items.how: A guaranteed commercial loan prepays costlier loans; most of the savings build secondary schools.
items.label: 30 more secondary schools

items.name: Debt-for-Development Swap
items.headline: Costly commercial debt bought back; the savings fund education.
items.how: A World Bank guarantee stands behind a cheaper, longer loan that buys back the most expensive commercial debt.
items.label: about EUR 330M freed for schools

items.name: Debt Restructuring
items.headline: Old bonds exchanged for new ones on easier terms.
items.how: Bondholders swap their bonds for new ones with longer maturities or less principal, so the nation can pay.
items.label: of external debt exchanged

families.name: Disaster risk finance
families.line: Money agreed before the storm, paid within weeks of it.

items.name: Catastrophe Bond
items.headline: Investors pay the nation when a disaster crosses a trigger.
items.how: Investors earn a premium; if a storm or earthquake crosses an agreed threshold, their principal goes to the nation.
items.label: paid in full after Hurricane Melissa

items.name: Parametric Risk Pool
items.headline: Nations pool disaster risk and pay less for cover.
items.how: Member governments buy cover together; payouts follow measured wind, rain or quake readings, with no claims process.
items.label: CCRIF’s largest single payout, after Hurricane Melissa

items.name: Sovereign Drought Insurance
items.headline: Cover that pays when the rains fail.
items.how: Payouts follow measured rainfall, so food reaches families within weeks of a failed season.
items.label: released after the El Niño drought

items.name: Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option
items.headline: A credit line that opens the day disaster strikes.
items.how: The loan is agreed in calm times and drawn the moment a disaster is declared.
items.label: after the August earthquake

items.name: Climate-Resilient Debt Clause
items.headline: Debt payments pause for two years after a disaster.
items.how: A clause in the bond defers payments after a severe hurricane, flood or epidemic, so the budget can go to recovery.
items.label: a benchmark-size global bond

families.name: Trade and commodity finance
families.line: Short-term money that keeps food, fuel and exports moving.

items.name: Trade Finance Facility
items.headline: Funds for a nation’s imports of fuel and food.
items.how: A trade finance lender pays for a state buyer’s imports, repaid within months from sales.
items.label: planned for fuel and strategic food imports
items.source: Ministry of Planning, Economic Development and International Cooperation of Egypt, February 2025

items.name: Trade Finance Guarantee
items.headline: Lets local banks finance small importers and exporters.
items.how: The development bank covers a bank’s risk on trade deals, so small firms get credit.
items.label: up to 100% of eligible trade covered

items.name: Commodity Risk Participation
items.headline: Shares the risk of crop finance, so banks lend to farmers.
items.how: The development bank takes part of the risk on a bank’s loans to crop buyers, without lending itself.
items.label: traceable cocoa from 139,000+ smallholders

items.name: Import Finance Facility
items.headline: Foreign currency set aside for life-saving imports.
items.how: A grant-funded facility at the central bank pays for strategic imports when foreign exchange runs short.
items.label: for fertiliser and medicine imports

families.name: Grants and climate funds
families.line: Money that does not have to be repaid.

items.name: Development Grant
items.headline: Grants for the poorest nations, never repaid.
items.how: IDA and similar windows give grants to nations at high risk of debt distress.
items.label: for water and sanitation

items.name: Climate Fund Grant
items.headline: Climate funds pay to restore land and forests.
items.how: Funds such as the Green Climate Fund give grants for adaptation and for cutting emissions.
items.label: to restore savanna forest and shea parklands

items.name: Forest Investment Fund
items.headline: Pays nations every year to keep forests standing.
items.how: A fund invests its capital and pays tropical forest nations for each hectare kept standing.
items.label: committed by September 2026

items.name: Multi-Donor Trust Fund
items.headline: Donors pool grants behind one programme.
items.how: A trust fund run by a development bank pays for basic services under one set of rules.
items.label: for basic services, outside the authorities

items.name: Humanitarian Appeal
items.headline: Appeals fund food, water and shelter in a crisis.
items.how: The UN and its partners publish what a year of relief will cost, and donors fund it.
items.label: for 17.5 million people targeted
